Module 3: Repeating Tasks (Loops)

3.1 range() Function:
The range() Function
Imagine you had to write down all the numbers from 1 to 1,000. Typing that by hand would take forever and get really boring!
Luckily, Python has a built-in magic number-generator called the range() function.
Instead of writing out numbers one by one, range() instantly generates a sequence of whole numbers for you:
Output
The Golden "Stop-Before" Rule
In range(start, stop), Python starts at the start number, but stops one step before reaching the stop number! That is why range(2, 7) stops at 6, not 7.
Click Next Lesson to see what happens when you give range() only one number!
range() with One Argument
When you pass only one single number into range(), Python assumes that number is the stop value, and it automatically starts counting from 0:
Output
Why Coders Love Starting at 0
Computers are built around zero-based indexing. Passing range(n) runs your loop exactly n times (from 0 to n - 1).
Quiz: Single Argument range()
What will be the output of the following code?
Tap an option below to answer:

| A: 1 2 3 on separate lines |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! With one argument, range() always starts counting at 0, not 1. |

| B: 0 1 2 on separate lines |
| Correct Answer! 🎉
range(3) starts at 0 and generates 3 numbers: 0, 1, and 2 (stopping before 3). |

| C: 0 1 2 3 on separate lines |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Remember the stop-before rule: the stop number 3 is excluded. |

| D: 3 |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! range() produces a sequence of numbers, not just the stop value. |
The Step Argument
What if you don’t want to count by ones? What if you want to count by twos, fives, or tens?
You can add a third number called the step:
Think of the step like playing hopscotch—it tells Python how many tiles to skip forward on each jump:
Output
Here, Python starts at 2, adds 2 each time (), and stops before reaching 11.
Practice: Multiples of Five
Problem Description
Write a program using range() with the step argument to print the multiples of 5 from 5 up to 25 (including 25).
Hints:
start is 5
step is 5
Remember the stop-before rule: to include 25, your stop value should be 26 or 30!
for num in range(5, 26, 5):
Example:
Reverse Sequence (Counting Backwards)
You can also use range() to count backwards!
To make a countdown sequence:
Make your start number larger than your stop number.
Use a negative number for the step (like -1 or -2):
Output
How It Works:
Python starts at 5, subtracts 1 each turn, and stops right before reaching 0 (so 1 is the last number printed).
Practice: Arcade Countdown Timer
Problem Description
A game shows a 10-second warning countdown before the gates close.
Write a program using range() that counts down backwards from 10 to 1 by ones, and prints Time is up! after the loop finishes.
Hints:
Use range(10, 0, -1)
Put print("Time is up!") outside the loop without indentation.

3.2 Python for Loop
Introduction to Loops
Imagine your coach asks you to do 50 jumping jacks. You do one, count in your head, do another, count again, and keep repeating until you reach 50.
In programming, when you want your computer to repeat an action again and again, you use a loop.

Without loops, if you wanted to print a message 100 times, you would have to write print() 100 times! With a loop, you write the instruction once, and Python repeats it 10, 1,000, or even a million times in the blink of an eye.
Click Next Lesson to meet our first loop: the while loop!
The while Loop
A while loop repeats a block of code as long as a condition remains True.
Think of it like a parent saying: "While your room is messy, keep cleaning!"
Basic Syntax:
Figure: Check Condition
The Rule of the Counter:
If the condition never becomes False, the loop will run forever (an infinite loop!). To stop the loop, you must change something inside the loop—like updating a counter variable (count += 1).
Example: The while Loop
Let’s watch a counter loop from 1 to 4:
Output
Step-by-Step Breakdown:
Turn 1: count is 1 ( is True). Prints Lap 1. count becomes 2.
Turn 2: count is 2 ( is True). Prints Lap 2. count becomes 3.
Turn 3: count is 3 ( is True). Prints Lap 3. count becomes 4.
Turn 4: count is 4 ( is True). Prints Lap 4. count becomes 5.
Turn 5: count is 5 ( is False). The loop stops, and the race finishes!
Quiz: Counting Loop Turns
How many times will print("Sparky") run in this program?
Tap an option below to answer:

| A: 2 times |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Trace the values: pet_count will be 0, 1, and 2 before reaching 3. |

| B: 3 times |
| Correct Answer! 🎉 The loop runs for pet_count = 0, pet_count = 1, and pet_count = 2. When it hits 3, the condition 3 < 3 becomes False! |

| C: 4 times |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Because the operator is < (strictly less than), 3 is not included. |

| D: Infinite times |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! pet_count += 1 updates the variable each turn, so it will safely stop. |

Write a while loop with the condition i <= 5.
Inside the loop, print Go Team! 📣 and increase i by 1 (i += 1).

Sometimes you don't know in advance how many times a loop should run. You want it to keep asking the user questions until they choose to stop!
A special stopping value is called a sentinel value (like typing 0 or "exit"):
Sample Output
When the user types quit, the condition word != "quit" becomes False, and the loop gracefully ends!
Example: Sum of Numbers Until 0
Let’s build an interactive calculator that adds up numbers entered by the user until they type 0:
Sample Output
Quiz: The Accumulator Trap
What is wrong with this code designed to sum numbers?
Tap an option below to answer:

| A: total += number is invalid syntax. |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! += is completely valid Python shorthand. |

| B: total = 0 is inside the loop, so it resets every turn. |
| Correct Answer! 🎉 Putting total = 0 inside the loop erases the sum on every turn! An accumulator must always be initialized before/outside the loop. |

| C: The while condition cannot compare with 0. |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! number != 0 is a standard comparison. |

| D: A NameError will occur. |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! total is defined inside, but it loses previous additions. |

Problem Description
You are counting coins in a digital piggy bank! Write a program that keeps asking the user to deposit coins (in cents) until they enter 0.

Use a while coin != 0: loop:
Add coin to savings.

After the loop ends, print: Total saved in bank: [savings] cents.

3.3 Python while Loop

For Loop

In the previous lesson, you used a while loop to repeat code as long as a condition was true.

Now, meet Python's most popular loop: the for loop!

A for loop is built to travel through a sequence of items one by one from start to finish.

Think of it like an amusement park ride inspector checking each roller-coaster cart in order:

Check Cart 1

Check Cart 2

Check Cart 3

All done!

Whenever you have a list, a word, or a range of numbers, a for loop visits each item automatically without you having to manually manage counters!

Click Next Lesson to see a for loop in action.

Example: The for Loop

You already know that text strings are made of individual letters arranged in order. That makes a string a sequence!

Watch what happens when we loop through a word:

Output

Why Did It Run 4 Times?

Because "Nova" has 4 letters (N, o, v, a). For each character in the string, the for loop runs its indented code once!

Access Elements

A for loop doesn’t just repeat code—it lets you inspect the exact element it is currently looking at!

In for letter in hero_name:, the variable letter holds a new character on every single turn:

Output

Turn 1: char is "B"

Turn 2: char is "o"

Turn 3: char is "l"

Turn 4: char is "t"

You can name this loop variable anything you want (like letter, char, or item).

Quiz: Tracking Loop Elements

Look at the following code:

What is the value of letter during the 3rd iteration (turn) of the loop?

Tap an option below to answer:

| A: T |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! "T" is the 1st character of the string. |

| B: i |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! "i" is the 2nd character of the string. |

| C: g |
| Correct Answer! 🎉 In the 3rd iteration, the loop visits the 3rd letter of "Tiger", which is "g". |

| D: Tiger |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! The loop variable holds one single character at a time, not the entire word. |

Practice: Secret Spy Spelling

Problem Description

A secret spy agency transmits codenames letter-by-letter over radio:

Ask the user to enter a secret codename: code = input("Enter codename: ").

Use a for loop to inspect each character in code.

Print: Letter: followed by that character.

Example:

List Sequence

In Python, the most famous sequence of all is a List.

A list allows you to store multiple items inside a single variable! You create a list by placing items inside square brackets [ ] separated by commas:

Output

Figure: A backpack with 3 labeled slots holding 'Apple', 'Mango', and 'Banana'

Click Next Lesson to see how a for loop explores a list!

Iterate Over a List

Using a for loop to visit every item in a list is called iteration. It's the cleanest way to process collections of data:

Output

Python automatically starts at the first item, moves through to the last, and stops cleanly when finished!

The range() Sequence

What if you want to loop a set number of times without writing a list of words?

That’s where range() comes in! range() produces an automated sequence of numbers ready for a for loop:

Click Next Lesson to combine for loops with range()!

Using for Loop with range()

Combining for with range() is the standard way to count in Python:

Output

Notice how clean this is compared to a while loop: no counter setup (i = 1) and no manual updating (i += 1) needed!

Quiz: Loop with range()

What will be displayed by this code?

Tap an option below to answer:

| A: 3 4 5 6 7 |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Don't forget that inside the loop, the code prints num + 1! |

| B: 4 5 6 7 |
| Correct Answer! 🎉 range(3, 7) generates . Adding  to each prints ! |

| C: 4 5 6 7 8 |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Remember that range(3, 7) excludes the stop value 7. |

| D: 3 4 5 6 |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! The code adds 1 to each number before printing. |

Practice: Counting Up to n

Problem Description

Write a program that takes an integer n from the user and prints all numbers starting from 0 up to n - 1 using range(n).

Hints:

n = int(input("Enter number: "))

for i in range(n):

print(i)

Sum of Natural Numbers

Natural numbers are the positive counting numbers:

Suppose you want to find the sum of all natural numbers up to :

How do we teach a computer to calculate this for any number  (even up to )?

We use the accumulator pattern with a for loop!

Click Next Lesson to see the step-by-step logic.

Logic to Find Sum of Natural Numbers

Here are the 4 logical steps:

Get  from the user: n = int(input("Enter n: "))

Initialize total outside the loop: total = 0 (your basket starts empty).

Loop from 1 to : Use range(1, n + 1) so  is included!

Add to total on each turn: total += i

Sample Output

Practice: Product of Numbers (Factorial)

Problem Description

The product of all numbers from  up to  is called a Factorial ():

Write a program that:

Takes a positive integer: n = int(input("Enter positive integer: ")).

Starts an accumulator named product = 1 (start at 1, because multiplying by 0 gives 0!).

Loops through range(1, n + 1) and multiplies: product *= i.

Prints product after the loop.

Example:

Using if Statement Inside a Loop

What if you want to examine numbers in a loop and only print the ones that meet a special condition?

You can place an if statement directly inside your for loop!

Let's find all even numbers between  and :

Output

On odd numbers, num % 2 == 0 is False, so Python quietly skips the print()!

Quiz: Filtering Inside Loops

What will be displayed by this code?

Tap an option below to answer:

| A: 5 10 15 |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Remember the stop-before rule: range(1, 15) stops at 14, so 15 is never reached. |

| B: 5 10 |
| Correct Answer! 🎉 Only 5 and 10 are multiples of 5 within the range from 1 to 14! |

| C: 0 5 10 |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! range(1, 15) starts at 1, not 0. |

| D: All numbers from 1 to 14 |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! The if condition filters out all numbers that are not divisible by 5. |

Practice: Multiples of 3 Hunter

Problem Description

Write a program that prints all numbers divisible by 3 between 1 and n (inclusive):

Ask the user for an integer: n = int(input("Enter maximum number: ")).

Use a for loop through range(1, n + 1).

Inside the loop, check if num % 3 == 0.

If True, print num.

Scenario

A track-and-field junior athlete runs 5 practice laps. Their coach timed each lap in seconds:

The coach wants to find all laps that were faster than 60 seconds (time < 60) to award speed badges:

Loop through lap_times using a for loop.

Check if lap < 60 with an if statement, and print the qualified lap.

Outside the loop, print the completion message.

3.4 Loop Controls (break and continue)

Introduction

Usually, a loop runs until its condition becomes False or until it reaches the end of a list.

But in real-world programs, unexpected things happen:

What if a game character loses all lives? You want to stop the game loop immediately, without waiting for the timer to run out!

What if an inspection robot spots a cracked egg on a conveyor belt? You want to skip packing that one egg and jump straight to the next one!

To take precise control of your loops, Python provides two special steering wheels:

break: The Emergency Brake (stops and exits the loop immediately).

continue: The Skip Button (skips the rest of the current turn and jumps to the next turn).

Click Next Lesson to learn about break!

The break Statement

The break statement immediately stops a loop in its tracks. As soon as Python hits break, it abandons the loop completely and jumps down to the code outside the loop!

Output

Notice What Happened:

Even though range(1, 10) was ready to count all the way to 9, as soon as number reached 4, break ran, and the loop stopped instantly!

Break with if...else Statement

In real code, break is almost always placed inside an if statement to look for a specific trigger condition.

Let’s search for a target item in an inventory:

Output

Once the key was found, there was no need to check "Torch" or "Rope"—the loop exited right away!

Quiz: Evaluating break

How many times will print("Scanning...") run in this code?

Tap an option below to answer:

| A: 8 times |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! break stops the loop early when i == 3. |

| B: 7 times |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! range(1, 8) would run 7 times normally, but the break cuts it short. |

| C: 3 times |
| Correct Answer! 🎉 It prints for i = 1, i = 2, and i = 3. Right after printing on turn 3, the if i == 3 trigger fires the break! |

| D: 2 times |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Notice that the print() statement comes before the if check. |

Practice: Stop at Multiples of 5

Problem Description

Write a program that prints numbers from 1 to 20, but stops the moment it reaches a number divisible by 5:

Loop through range(1, 21).

Print the current number.

If the number is divisible by 5 (num % 5 == 0), exit the loop using break.

Example:

Example: The while True + break Pattern

Professional developers often create loops using while True: (an intentional infinite loop) and use break to exit when the user types a quit command:

Sample Output

This pattern is much cleaner than writing complicated while conditions!

The continue Statement

While break completely quits the loop, continue simply skips the rest of the current turn and jumps straight to the next one!

Think of it like a music player hitting the "Next Track" button:

break = Pressing STOP (music shuts off completely).

continue = Pressing SKIP (skips only this song and plays the next).

Figure: continue triggered ---> Skip remaining lines below ---> Jump to next turn of loop

Click Next Lesson to see continue in action!

Example: The continue Statement

Let’s print numbers from 1 to 5, but skip the unlucky number 3:

Output

What Happened to 3?

When num was 3, continue ran. Python immediately skipped print(num) and leaped right to num = 4!

Quiz: Predicting continue Output

What will be displayed by this code?

Tap an option below to answer:

| A: P Y T H O N on separate lines |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! When letter == "H", continue skips the print() statement for that letter. |

| B: P Y T on separate lines |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! continue does not stop the loop like break—it keeps going with "O" and "N". |

| C: P Y T O N on separate lines |
| Correct Answer! 🎉 Only "H" is skipped! The loop continues running and finishes printing "O" and "N". |

| D: An error occurs. |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! continue is standard, valid Python inside any loop. |

Practice: Skip Multiples of 3

Problem Description

Write a program that loops through numbers from 1 to 10:

Use a for loop with range(1, 11).

If a number is divisible by 3 (num % 3 == 0), skip it using continue.

Otherwise, print the number.

Example:

Example: Combining break and continue

Real-world algorithms frequently use both tools together!

Suppose an automated fruit sorter processes weights in grams:

If a fruit weight is negative (invalid sensor error), skip it using continue.

If a weight of 0 is seen (the conveyor belt has stopped), end the loop using break.

Otherwise, add the weight to our total shipment:

Output

(Calculates: . Skipped , stopped at , ignored  and ).

Quiz: break and continue Combo

Look at this code:

What numbers will be printed?

Tap an option below to answer:

| A: 2 4 6 8 |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Notice that x == 0 triggers a break, which prevents 8 from ever being processed. |

| B: 2 4 6 |
| Correct Answer! 🎉 2 and 4 print. 7 is odd, so continue skips it. 6 prints. 0 triggers break, stopping the loop immediately! |

| C: 2 4 7 6 |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! 7 % 2 != 0 is True, so continue skips 7. |

| D: 2 4 6 0 |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! 0 causes a break before reaching the print(x) statement. |

You are scoring an archery tournament:

Initialize total = 0.

Loop through scores:

If a score is negative (score < 0), skip it using continue.

lessons.summary: What happens when you put a loop inside another loop? You get a Nested Loop!

blocks.content: 3.5 Nested Loops
Introduction
What happens when you put a loop inside another loop? You get a Nested Loop!
Think of real-life examples where one cycle contains another smaller cycle:
A Clock: For every 1 hour that passes (outer loop), the minute hand must cycle through 60 minutes (inner loop).
A Calendar: For each month (outer loop), you live through all 30 days (inner loop).
Sports Practice: Your coach tells you to do 3 sets (outer loop) of 5 jumping jacks (inner loop).
In Python:
The Outer Loop controls how many big rounds you do.
The Inner Loop runs completely from start to finish on every single turn of the outer loop!
Click Next Lesson to see how Python runs a nested loop!
Example: The Nested Loop
Let’s watch a workout coach program with 2 sets of 3 pushups:
Output
The Golden Math Rule of Nested Loops:
Here,  completed!
Quiz: Total Iterations
How many times in total will print("Sparkle ✨") execute in this code?
Tap an option below to answer:

| A: 7 times |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Don't add the numbers (). Remember that the inner loop runs completely for every turn of the outer loop! |

| B: 12 times |
| Correct Answer! 🎉 The outer loop runs 3 times, and for each of those 3 times, the inner loop runs 4 times:  total times! |

| C: 4 times |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! The inner loop runs 4 times per outer turn, not just once. |

| D: 3 times |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! 3 is only the number of outer loop turns. |
Quiz: Variable Values in Nested Loops
Look at this nested loop:
What will be the exact output?
Tap an option below to answer:

| A: 1A 2B |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! For row = 1, the inner loop must finish both "A" and "B" before row can become 2. |

| B: 1A 1B 2A 2B on separate lines |
| Correct Answer! 🎉 When row is 1, col runs through "A" and "B" (1A, 1B). Then row becomes 2, and col runs through "A" and "B" again (2A, 2B)! |

| C: 12 AB on separate lines |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! The print statement combines the current row and col together. |

| D: An IndentationError occurs. |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! The double indentation for the inner loop is formatted properly. |
Practice: Treasure Map Coordinates
Problem Description
A video game map has a grid with 2 rows and 3 columns. Write a program using nested for loops to display every tile coordinate on the map:
Outer loop: for row in range(1, 3): (Rows 1 and 2).
Inner loop: for col in range(1, 4): (Columns 1, 2, and 3).
Inside the inner loop, print: Tile: (row, col).

Module 3 Wrap-Up & Milestone Unlocked! 🏆
🎉 MASSIVE CONGRATULATIONS! 🎉
You have officially conquered Module 3: Repetition & Sequences!

When you started, your code could only run in a straight line or make single choices. Now, you have unlocked the power of automation—making your computer repeat tasks thousands of times without breaking a sweat!
Recap
Your Module 3 Superpowers Recap:
The range() Machine: Instantly generates number sequences forward, with custom steps, or counting backwards (range(start, stop, step)).
The while Loop: Keeps running as long as a condition is True—perfect for games, battery chargers, and countdowns.
The Sentinel Loop: Keeps asking for user input until they decide to stop (like typing 0 or "quit").
The for Loop: Glides effortlessly through text strings, lists, and number sequences.
The Accumulator Pattern: Collects totals, sums natural numbers, and computes factorials (total += item).
Loop Controls:
break: The emergency brake that stops a loop instantly.
continue: The skip button that hops past bad data to the next turn.
Nested Loops: Puts loops inside loops to scan grids, coordinates, and multi-round workout sets.
Up Next: Module 4 — Storing & Organizing Collections 🎒
Until now, each of our variables held just one value at a time (like score = 100 or name = "Aria"). But what if you’re building a video game and need to store:
An inventory of 50 potions, swords, and shields?
A leaderboard of top 100 player scores?
A player profile matching usernames to secret passcodes?
In Module 4: Storing & Organizing Collections, you’ll learn Python's ultimate storage tools:
Lists ([ ]): Ordered, flexible backpacks where you can add, remove, and sort items.
Tuples (( )): Locked treasure chests for coordinates and permanent data that never changes.
Dictionaries ({ }): Super-fast lookup phonebooks that link keys to values (like {"Hero": "SuperNova", "Health": 100}).
Click Start Module 4 to step into Storing & Organizing Collections!
